title: How many ways to order four tasks?
hook: Some tasks must wait for others. Is there one right order, several, or maybe none?

doesNotKnow: that dependencies can allow several valid orders, and that a loop of dependencies allows none

misconception: Tasks with dependencies have only one valid order, or every set of dependencies can be satisfied.
objective: The learner can build both valid orders of A before B, A before C, B before D, C before D (A B C D and A C B D) by repeatedly taking a free task, and explain why adding D before A leaves no order.

claims.text: With A before B, A before C, B before D and C before D, exactly 2 orders of all four tasks obey every rule: A B C D and A C B D.
claims.source: Demo.tsx VALID: brute force over all 24 permutations. Builder re-ran the same filter in Node: [ABCD, ACBD].

claims.text: Taking, again and again, any task with nothing left before it builds a valid order.
claims.source: Kahn, 'Topological sorting of large networks', CACM 5(11), 1962; CLRS (3rd ed.) 22.4 and exercise 22.4-5.

claims.text: After A, both B and C are free, and that choice is the only freedom, so there are exactly 2 orders.
claims.source: A is the only task with no arrows in, so it is first; D needs B and C, so it is last; B and C have no arrow between them, giving 2 ways. Matches c1.

claims.text: With D before A added, every task waits for another, so nothing can go first: a loop has no order at all.
claims.source: A directed graph has a topological order iff it has no cycle (CLRS 22.4, Lemma 22.11). Here A→B→D→A is a cycle; every node has an incoming arrow (A from D, B and C from A, D from B and C).

claims.text: Swapping neighbours in a valid line is allowed only if no arrow joins them (A B C D: swapping A and B or B and D breaks an arrow; swapping B and C gives A C B D).
claims.source: Swapping adjacent x, y changes only their relative order, so it is valid iff there is no arrow x→y. Demo.tsx swap().

recall.question: Tasks: X before Y, Y before Z, Z before X. How many orders obey every rule?
recall.why: The rules form a loop: every task waits for another, so no task can go first and no order exists.
